summary: This document gives best current practice for dropping or marking packets with any active queue management (AQM) algorithm, including RED, BLUE, PCN, CoDel, and PIE. It addresses whether congestion signals should depend on packet size or count.

eli5.summary: When a line is too long, you have to pick whom to turn away. This says whether big or small items should be turned away more, so it is fair.

questions: should aqm drop depend on packet size
what is byte mode drop in red
why not drop small packets less often
subtitle: Should a congested router treat small and large packets differently when it drops or marks them? This BCP says no.

tldr.problem: Active queue management can make the chance of dropping or marking a packet depend on its size, and earlier advice in the RFC series was conflicting about whether it should.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits congestion notification into three stages: measuring congestion, encoding it in drops or marks, and decoding it at the transport. Measurement should follow what actually congests the resource, the network's drop or mark probability should ignore packet size, and the transport should treat the signal as proportional to the size of the packet.
tldr.outcome: RED's byte-mode drop variant should not be used, and the RFC updates RFC 2309 and RFC 2914. A limited vendor survey found no one had implemented byte-mode drop, so deprecating it should cost little.

today: RFC 7141 is a Best Current Practice and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 2309 and RFC 2914.

sections.title: The Byte vs Packet Question
sections.content:
When a network signals congestion, there is a long-running question about packet size. The RFC says it arises at three stages: measuring congestion (should a queue be counted in time, bytes or packets?), encoding it (should the chance that a packet is dropped or marked depend on that packet's size?) and decoding it (should a transport weigh a lost or marked packet by its size?).

Consensus exists for the first stage. The controversy is about the last two. Before this memo, the RFC series was largely silent, apart from a paper trail of advice referenced from RFC 2309 that conditionally recommends byte-mode (packet-size dependent) drop.

The memo applies to all active queue management (AQM) algorithms, including RED, BLUE, PCN, CoDel and PIE. RED is used throughout as the worked example because it is widely known.
sections.eli5: There are three moments where size could matter: when you count how full the line is, when you decide who to turn away, and when the person turned away decides how much to slow down. People disagree most about the last two.

sections.title: Key Terms: Bit-Congestible and Packet-Congestible
sections.content:
A resource is bit-congestible if its load depends on the rate at which bits arrive, and packet-congestible if the load depends on the rate at which packets arrive. Transmission links, radio power and most buffer memory are bit-congestible. Route look-up engines and firewalls are packet-congestible, because they process one header per packet.

The memo also separates the two modes of RED. Packet-mode and byte-mode queue measurement count the queue in packets or bytes. Packet-mode drop drops a packet with a probability independent of its size, while byte-mode drop makes the probability depend on size. The RFC insists that these terms never be used without saying whether they apply to measurement or to drop.

It also notes that packet congestion is currently rare, because router designers size packet-processing engines to stay uncongested even under worst-case runs of minimum-size packets.
sections.eli5: A road can be busy because of the number of cars or because of how much they weigh in total. Which one matters depends on what is being squeezed, a toll booth that handles one car at a time, or a bridge that carries weight.

sections.title: Worked Example: Packet-Mode vs Byte-Mode Drop
sections.content:
Take two flows with the same bit rate of 48 Mbps. One uses 60 byte packets (100,000 packets per second) and the other uses 1,500 byte packets (4,000 packets per second). The small packets are 25 times smaller, so there are 25 times more of them.

With packet-mode drop at 0.1%, both flows lose 0.1% of their packets. That is 100 small packets and 4 large packets per second, but in both cases 48 kbps of bits. In effect every bit is dropped with the same probability, wherever it sits.

With byte-mode drop, the 0.1% applies only to maximum-size packets and the probability for small packets shrinks in proportion to size, to 0.004%. Both flows then lose 4 packets per second, but the small flow loses 1.92 kbps while the large flow loses 48 kbps. Small packets get a large discount.
sections.eli5: If a guard flips a coin for every person, a crowd of tiny kids loses as many kids as a few grown-ups lose grown-ups, and the same total size gets turned away. If the guard goes easy on small people, a crowd of tiny people gets through almost untouched.

sections.title: The Four Recommendations
sections.content:
Section 2 gives the formal advice. Queue measurement: if the AQM measures queue length, it SHOULD count bytes for a bit-congestible resource and packets for a packet-congestible one. For RED, an implementation SHOULD NOT let the operator configure how the queue measures itself, since that is an inherent property of the queue.

Encoding: the probability that equipment drops or marks a packet SHOULD NOT depend on the size of that packet. RED SHOULD NOT use byte-mode drop, and an operator who has turned it on is RECOMMENDED to switch to packet-mode drop. RED as a whole SHOULD NOT be switched off, since a tail-drop queue biases against large packets and is vulnerable to floods of small packets.

Responding: when a transport detects a lost or marked packet, it SHOULD treat the strength of the indication as proportionate to the packet's size in octets, as if each octet carried an indication. This only describes how to interpret the signal. It does not say the transport must act on it.

Splitting and merging: where packets carrying ECN marks are split or merged, the number of marked octets SHOULD be the same before and after.
sections.eli5: Count the line in whatever really fills it up. Let the guard treat everyone's turn the same. Let each person decide for themselves how much to slow down based on how big they were.

sections.title: Why Not Favour Small Packets
sections.content:
The motivating arguments are informative. The first is perverse incentives. A queue that favours small packets lets an attacker amplify a flood by sending many small packets, and it pushes honest senders to break their data into tiny segments to reduce their drop rate. The RFC gives a gentle RED example with two 1 Mbps unresponsive flows of 1,500 B and 60 B packets, where the large-packet flow is targeted for 750 kbps and the small-packet flow for 990 kbps.

The second is small is not control. Many control packets (TCP SYNs and ACKs, DNS messages, SIP messages) are small, but not all small packets are control packets. The RFC argues transports should be made robust against control-packet loss instead.

The third is a transport-independent network. To equalise bit rates for TCP, the network would have to assume how aggressively transports respond and assume a baseline packet size such as the local MTU. If the network never considers size, the transport receives two facts, the congestion signal and the packet size, and can combine them or not.

The fourth is partial deployment. Many cheap bridges, software firewalls and consumer NATs use simple tail-drop buffers, and any AQM must fall back to tail drop when the buffer is exhausted. A host cannot tell a deliberate AQM drop from a buffer-exhaustion drop, so the network cannot universally drop in proportion to size and should not try at all.

Finally, the RFC notes that size-dependent drop needs an extra multiply and divide in the network, which the transport can avoid.
sections.eli5: If small people get waved through, everyone will just shrink into tiny groups to sneak in. Also, a guard cannot treat everyone fairly if some doors have no guard at all. It is better if each person adjusts on their own.

sections.title: Past Advice and Where It Went Wrong
sections.content:
The original 1993 RED paper offered packet mode and byte mode. When RFC 2309 recommended RED in 1998, it left the choice open and pointed to a 1997 email for tuning advice. That advice said drop probability should depend on packet size if the resource is bit-congestible, so that a flow's share of drops indicated its share of bandwidth. The memo argues the real fix would have been for a policing mechanism to count bytes dropped, not packets.

An addendum to that email later said the size question is orthogonal to whether the resource is bit-congestible. Later work refined the size adjustment: De Cnodder and colleagues in 2000 proposed RED_4 and RED_5, and the ns2 simulator made a byte-mode variant its default on 10 November 2004. The RFC warns that ns2 results using RED without disabling byte-mode drop may differ greatly from production RED.

On the transport side, the RFC cites TFRC-SP (RFC 4828), a small-packet variant of TFRC that adjusts a flow's rate for packet size. It also cites TCP changes (RFC 5562 and RFC 5690) that make TCP more robust against losing control packets. A summary table shows that doing nothing, or adding the transport fix without any network bias, gives sensible results, while doing both biases rates far too much towards small packets.
sections.eli5: People once thought it was a good idea for the guard to go easy on small people. Over the years they found that it caused trouble, and that it works better if the people themselves adjust.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security argument is that biasing drops towards small packets creates a perverse incentive to chop flows into tiny segments, and it opens a vulnerability to small-packet DDoS attacks. AQM was meant to remove these weaknesses of tail-drop queues, so they should not be added back.

If most queues used byte-mode drop, a small-packet flood would push aside large packets at one queue after another while suffering much less drop itself, so the network would amplify its effect. The RFC adds that tail-drop queues amplify such attacks even more than byte-mode RED, so neither should be used where avoidable.

Appendix C explains that the ability of networks to police how any transport responds to congestion depends on bit-congestible resources doing only packet-mode drop.
sections.eli5: If small packets are favoured, a bully can send a flood of tiny ones and shove everybody else aside while barely getting stopped himself.

sections.title: Conclusions and Open Issues
sections.content:
The memo's three answers are 'it depends', 'no', and 'yes'. Measure in bytes or packets depending on what is congested, do not take packet size into account when dropping or marking, and do scale a transport's rate reduction with the size of the packet that signalled congestion.

For RED, this means byte-mode queue measurement is often appropriate and byte-mode drop is very strongly discouraged. The RFC reports a survey of 84 equipment vendors, of which 19% responded and none had implemented byte-mode drop in RED. It concludes that no migration strategy is really needed.

Open issues remain. The IETF should keep updating congestion control protocols to account for packet size, and should keep making protocols less sensitive to losing SYNs, pure ACKs and DNS exchanges. The position is less clear-cut if the Internet ever gets an even mix of packet-congestible and bit-congestible resources, a question the memo points to the IRTF's ICCRG and RFC 6077.
sections.eli5: The answers are: it depends what is crowded, no for the guard, and yes for the person who was turned away. Nobody really built the bad idea anyway, so there is little to clean up.

viz.caption: THE THREE STAGES AND THE ANSWER AT EACH

items.title: Measuring congestion
items.text: It depends: bytes for bit-congestible resources, packets for packet-congestible ones.

items.title: Encoding in drops or marks
items.text: No: the chance of drop or mark should not depend on packet size.

items.title: Decoding at the transport
items.text: Yes: treat the signal as proportional to the packet's size in octets.
